doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Coltrane, Blues People and Oberlin: music as connected to life
summary: Coltrane's music, Malcolm X, and Blues People led him to ask about Chinese railroad workers' songs, inspiring Great Wall Gold Mountain, with Ellington's Black, Brown and Beige and mentor Wendell Logan at Oberlin.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: is doing to other countries. But what was to me a turning point was when my cousin, who is currently an art professor and a friend of mine who is a drummer, introduced to me the music of John Coltrane. And even though I was not politically sophisticated or musically sophisticated at that time, I was only 17 or 18 years old, I was able to see how that music was connected — when I say — see I felt that music was connected with Malcolm X and later on I discovered that Malcolm X and that whole tradition of Harlem street corner oratorical style, Ed Davis, was connected with that music of John Coltrane and Albert Ayler and urban blues, and later on I discovered, even though I felt the connection of Martin Luther King with Gospel music and sermons, as Paul Robeson said, are sermons that are sung. So it was an incredible transformation and that’s why I say that that music became just as real to me, and maybe in some ways more important than Malcolm X because it was such on a high political level and I didn’t understand it. I mean they were words. I mean you’re 18 years old, 17, 18 years old, how are you going to understand it? Coltrane’s music, you didn’t really need to understand it to recognize its power. And so then I dropped out of UC Berkeley and I guess, oh yeah, the other part of the story is that when I was in high school a Stanford University grad student was teaching, then they called them alternative schools, was teaching in an alternative school class, a history class. And he knew I had some interest in music. So he gave me a book called Blues People by Leroi Jones, who is now called Amiri Baraka. And that changed me because the premise of that book is that as African-American people’s lives changed their music changed. And so in that book he talks about how Africans were brought over unwillingly to the United States and become slaves, and that they brought their songs over but the difference is that singing a song and working in your own land is different than singing a song working for somebody else’s land. So I thought about, and this is when I started thinking about my identity as a Chinese-American. Because there was I think Alex Haley’s “Roots” and searching for your roots, and that kind of climate that was popular. And so what happened when the Chinese came to the United States to build a railroad? Did they bring their songs? And did the context change? Now there’s no proof of that but that inspired me to write “Great Wall Gold Mountain,” which is on Tiananmen Recording, it’s the second movement. And it starts off with a Chinese work song that actually was inspired by another Chinese work song that was made I think it was in China, it was a Yen Ching work song, I think it was of the railroad, I can’t recall. And part of that work was inspired by Duke Ellington’s “Black, Brown and Beige” which he calls a tone parallel to African-American experience or life. And the first movement of that is “The Work Song.” And when I heard that music and the music that, this was introduced to me by Professor Wendell Logan. He was professor of African-American studies, jazz studies and contemporary music at the Oberlin Conservatory of Music. And

he served in sort of a mentor role. And so I was exposed to like “Black, Brown and Beige,” and a tone parallel to Harlem. And so I began to connect how music was part of life. And so I would say like my music is like an expression of my life. But as an American it means that I’m exposed to a diversity of influences and a younger generation of kids, through Internet, and they have access to a lot of opportunities.
